pharm: Reactivates organophosphate-inhibited acetylcholinesterase by removing the phosphoryl group
tags: Antidote for organophosphate poisoning and anticholinesterase overdose
Give WITH atropine, not instead of it
quick: Organophosphate poisoning: 1-2 g IV (in 100 mL saline over 15-30 min), repeat in 1 h then q6-12h as needed
Use if clearly needed; benefit in life-threatening poisoning outweighs limited data
Caution; single life-saving use generally acceptable - limited data
Renally excreted - reduce dose / extend interval in renal impairment
No specific adjustment established; use with general caution
Not relevant in acute antidotal use
Cardiac/ECG, neuromuscular status, respiration, blood pressure, cholinesterase levels if available
summary: Pralidoxime chloride (2-PAM) is a cholinesterase reactivator used as an antidote, together with atropine, for poisoning by organophosphate pesticides and chemicals (and certain anticholinesterase overdose, e.g. nerve agents). It reactivates acetylcholinesterase that has been inactivated by phosphorylation, relieving especially the nicotinic (skeletal-muscle) effects such as paralysis and respiratory muscle weakness that atropine does not address. It must be given as early as possible - generally little is achieved beyond about 36 hours after exposure, and reactivation fails once the enzyme has 'aged'. It is given by slow IV infusion (or IM/SC if IV not feasible) and is always an adjunct to, never a substitute for, atropine and supportive care.
indications: Treatment of poisoning by organophosphate pesticides and chemicals with anticholinesterase activity
Control of overdosage by anticholinesterase medications used to treat myasthenia gravis (e.g. neostigmine, pyridostigmine)
Adjunct (with atropine) to nerve-agent / organophosphate nerve poisoning

dosage.d: 1 to 2 g in 100 mL normal saline infused over 15-30 minutes
dosage.t: If pulmonary oedema or rapid bolus needed: give over not less than 5 minutes as ~50 mg/mL solution
dosage.n: Always with atropine; give as early as possible

dosage.d: Repeat the 1-2 g dose after about 1 hour if muscle weakness persists; then every 6-12 hours as needed
dosage.t: Severe/continued absorption may need continuous infusion

dosage.d: 20-50 mg/kg (up to ~2 g/dose) over 15-30 minutes; may repeat
dosage.t: Repeat in ~1 h, then q6-12h as needed

dosage.d: Initial 1-2 g, then 250 mg every 5 minutes as needed
600 mg IM per injection (e.g. DuoDote/ATNAA combination products), repeat per protocol

admin: Always administer with atropine and general supportive care (airway, decontamination, suction)
Preferred route is slow IV infusion in normal saline over 15-30 minutes
If giving by IV bolus, inject over not less than 5 minutes (rapid injection causes tachycardia, laryngospasm, muscle rigidity, transient neuromuscular block)
If IV access is not feasible, give intramuscularly or subcutaneously
Begin as soon as possible after exposure - benefit declines markedly after 36 hours and once the enzyme has aged
Continuously monitor cardiac rhythm and respiratory/neuromuscular status during administration
moa: Organophosphates and other anticholinesterase agents inhibit acetylcholinesterase by phosphorylating the enzyme's active site, causing acetylcholine accumulation and excessive cholinergic (muscarinic and nicotinic) stimulation. Pralidoxime is a quaternary oxime that attaches to the phosphorylated enzyme, then by nucleophilic attack cleaves the phosphorus-enzyme bond, removing the phosphoryl group and reactivating cholinesterase. Its most clinically important action is at nicotinic (skeletal-muscle) sites, relieving fasciculations and paralysis (including the muscles of respiration) - effects atropine does not reverse. It is ineffective once the inhibited enzyme has 'aged' (undergone irreversible dealkylation).

absolute: No known absolute contraindication when used as a life-saving antidote (relative contraindication: known hypersensitivity)
relative: Renal impairment (drug is renally excreted - reduce dose)
Myasthenia gravis being treated with anticholinesterases - pralidoxime may precipitate myasthenic crisis
Poisoning by carbamate (e.g. carbaryl) - pralidoxime may worsen toxicity; use with caution
Rapid IV administration (risk of tachycardia, laryngospasm, rigidity, transient apnoea)

preg: There are no adequate, well-controlled studies in pregnant women. In a life-threatening organophosphate poisoning, the benefit of treating the mother clearly outweighs the theoretical risk; pralidoxime should be used if indicated. Use only if clearly needed.
lact: It is not known whether pralidoxime is excreted in human milk. For a single emergency antidotal use it is generally considered acceptable; with repeated dosing, consider temporarily interrupting breastfeeding. Limited data.
renal: Pralidoxime is excreted largely unchanged in the urine. In renal impairment, clearance is reduced and the drug may accumulate - reduce the dose and/or extend the dosing interval and monitor for cholinergic-blocking/neuromuscular adverse effects.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established for hepatic impairment; use with general caution and standard supportive monitoring.

major: Barbiturates (potentiated by anticholinesterases - use with caution in mixed poisoning)
Morphine, theophylline, aminophylline, succinylcholine, reserpine, phenothiazines (avoid in organophosphate poisoning - worsen toxicity/respiratory depression)
moderate: Atropine (used together - watch for atropinisation signs which may appear earlier when pralidoxime is co-administered)
minor: None of major clinical significance in the acute setting
interactions.alcohol: Not relevant to acute antidotal use
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor plasma and RBC cholinesterase to assess reactivation; transient AST/ALT and CK elevations can occur

serious: Laryngospasm and muscle rigidity (with rapid IV injection)
Hypertensive episode (dose-related, can be reversed with IV phentolamine)
Excessive atropinisation when combined with atropine
rare: Transient elevation of hepatic transaminases and creatine kinase
emergency: Laryngospasm / acute respiratory compromise after rapid IV push
The underlying organophosphate cholinergic crisis itself (respiratory failure, seizures)

monitoring: Continuous cardiac/ECG monitoring during and after administration
Respiratory function and neuromuscular strength (response of muscle paralysis)
Blood pressure (transient pralidoxime-induced rise; reversible with phentolamine)
Signs of atropinisation (dry mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia) to titrate atropine
counsel: This is an emergency hospital antidote given by injection alongside atropine
Treatment works best when started as soon as possible after the poisoning
You may temporarily feel dizzy, have blurred vision, headache, or a fast heartbeat
Removal of contaminated clothing and skin washing (decontamination) is essential
Continued observation is needed because some organophosphates are absorbed slowly and toxicity can recur
Tell staff about all chemicals/pesticides involved and the time of exposure
pk: Reactivation of cholinesterase and relief of muscle weakness within minutes to hours when given early
Peak plasma levels within ~5-15 minutes after IV; ~10-20 minutes after IM
Approximately 0.8 to 2.7 hours (short; prolonged in renal impairment)
Short-acting - repeated dosing or continuous infusion needed for ongoing organophosphate exposure
Store at controlled room temperature (20-25 degrees C); reconstitute/dilute before use
pearls: Give WITH atropine - pralidoxime is an adjunct that addresses nicotinic (muscle/respiratory) effects; atropine treats muscarinic effects. It is never a substitute for atropine.
Time-critical: most effective within the first hours; little benefit after about 36 hours, and useless once the enzyme has 'aged' (irreversible).
Give slowly (IV over 15-30 min, or bolus over >=5 min) - rapid injection causes tachycardia, laryngospasm, rigidity, and transient apnoea.
Renally excreted - reduce dose in renal impairment.
Generally avoided/ineffective and possibly harmful in pure carbamate (e.g. carbaryl) poisoning.
Single-agent pralidoxime (Protopam Chloride) differs from combination auto-injectors (DuoDote/ATNAA) that pair pralidoxime with atropine for field nerve-agent use.
missed: Not applicable - pralidoxime is an acute parenteral antidote administered by clinicians, not a self-administered scheduled medication. Dosing is titrated to clinical response under medical supervision.
overdose: Excessive dosing or rapid administration can cause dizziness, blurred vision, diplopia, headache, nausea, tachycardia, hyperventilation, transient hypertension, and muscle weakness or neuromuscular blockade. Management is supportive: slow or stop the infusion, support ventilation as needed, and treat a severe hypertensive reaction with IV phentolamine. Distinguishing pralidoxime side effects from worsening organophosphate toxicity (or excessive atropinisation) requires careful clinical assessment.
